To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the growth in biological sequence databases is exponential; (2) the number of protein sequences in the databases has grown faster than DNA sequences and RNA sequences; (3) the number of organisms represented in the database is increasing; (4) the average length of DNA, RNA, and protein sequences is increasing; and (5) the number of proteins in each organism is increasing.

(i) the growth rate of sequence databases is increasing exponentially; (ii) there is an increase in the rate at which the growth rate is increasing; (iii) the rate at which growth is increasing is itself growing exponentially; (iv) the doubling time for the number of sequences is decreasing exponentially; and (v) this trend is expected to continue.

1) The number of biological sequences submitted to public biological databases has increased by an exponential rate of doubling every 15 to18 years; 2) The number of organisms from which biological sequences were derived has increased by a linear rate; 3) The number of species from which biological sequences have been derived has increased by an exponentially rate; 4) The number of sequences submitted by a single organism (human, mouse, yeast) has increased by an almost linear rate; 5)
